title: Case Study — Blockchain Certificate Verification
description: Read the case study scenario below and select the correct outcome when verifying a tampered certificate.
problem_statement:
CASE STUDY

EduVerify University issues thousands of digital certificates to students every year. These certificates are used by students when applying for jobs, internships, and higher studies.

The university faces a problem: some people have started editing digital certificates using image-editing software. For example, a student might change their grade from B to A or change the course name before submitting the certificate to a company.

To solve this problem, the university introduces a blockchain-based certificate verification system.

When a genuine certificate is issued:
• The university creates the digital certificate.
• A unique hash is generated for the certificate.
• This hash is stored on the university's blockchain.
• The student receives the certificate along with a QR code.

When a company scans the QR code, the system checks the certificate against the information stored on the blockchain.

One day, Rahul receives a certificate showing that he received a B grade.

Before applying for a job, Rahul edits the digital certificate and changes his grade from B to A. He does not have access to the university's blockchain system. He submits the modified certificate to a company.

What is most likely to happen when the company verifies Rahul's modified certificate?

options: A. The certificate will be accepted because Rahul's certificate number and name are still correct.
B. The certificate will be rejected because changing the grade changes the certificate's hash, which will no longer match the original hash stored on the blockchain.
C. The blockchain will automatically update the stored certificate and change Rahul's original grade from B to A.
D. The certificate will be accepted because blockchain only stores information and cannot detect changes made to digital documents.
acceptable_answers: The certificate will be rejected because changing the grade changes the certificate's hash, which will no longer match the original hash stored on the blockchain.
data.explanation: Option B is correct. Blockchain verification relies on cryptographic hashes. Any modification to the digital document (like changing a grade from B to A) alters its hash completely. The newly calculated hash will not match the original hash stored immutably on the blockchain, causing verification to fail and reject the certificate.
